titre_video: The US Treasury Is Trapped. A $1 Trillion Interest Collapse Begins NOW

segments.titre: Stacking loan on loan: the double standard
segments.resume: A person who stacked loan on top of loan every month just to survive would be cut off by the bank, have assets seized and life ruined. When the US government does the same thing, it is called fiscal policy. The opening sets up the double standard between citizens and the state.
segments.texte: If you stacked loan on top of loan every month, just to survive, the bank would cut you off. They’d seize your assets. They’d ruin your life. But when the US government does it… they call it fiscal policy.

segments.titre: Almost $3 billion a day goes to interest
segments.resume: America burns through almost $3 billion of taxpayer money every day, and it funds nothing: it only pays the interest on existing debt. The government is described as stuck in an economic death spiral, looking for an escape route in the public's bank accounts.
segments.texte: Right now, America burns through almost $3 billion of taxpayer money every single day. That money doesn’t fund anything. It just pays off the interest on debt. The government is stuck in an economic death spiral now and they’re scrambling for an escape route… Your bank account.

segments.titre: 15 years of free money and $28 trillion of debt in 2021
segments.resume: For 15 years the Federal Reserve kept the economy on a financial IV of free money, and people bragged about remortgaging. In 2021 the debt hit $28 trillion at an average rate of 1.5%, with only $352 billion of interest for the year, so borrowing felt like a cheat code and the borrowing continued.
segments.texte: For 15 years, the Federal Reserve had the U.S. economy hooked up to a financial IV. Free money was pumped into the system constantly. Interest rates were so low people were bragging about remortgaging their homes. It was like getting a lottery win. And Washington got in on the act. In 2021, the country’s debt had hit $28 trillion, but no one was worried. The average interest rate was sitting at a low 1.5%, so borrowing cash felt like a cheat code. The entire year's interest payment was $352 billion. For a superpower, it was pocket money. Everyone thought the good times would continue, so the borrowing continued. Debt was stacked on top of debt.

segments.titre: 2022: $30 trillion and the pandemic handouts
segments.resume: By 2022 the national debt passed $30 trillion for the first time. The pandemic blew a hole in the budget and the handouts stopped an economic collapse, but the terms on which the government borrowed that cash caused the real damage.
segments.texte: By 2022, the national debt passed $30 trillion for the first time. The pandemic blew a hole in the budget. As small businesses and critical infrastructure struggled to stay afloat, the government had to act. The handouts worked, stopping an economic collapse, but the terms the government borrowed that cash on caused the real damage.

segments.titre: Short-term borrowing: the teaser-rate mortgage for a whole country
segments.resume: Washington can lock money in at a fixed rate for 30 years or borrow short term, due in months and rolled over. It took huge amounts of the cheaper short-term money, like a teaser-rate mortgage that resets to market rates, the deal that cost many Americans their homes in 2008. Politicians never cut budgets, so the country gambled on rates staying low forever.
segments.texte: Every time Washington borrows money, it comes with a timeframe. Money can be locked in at a fixed rate for 30 years, just like a mortgage. Or it can be a short term, fast loan that can be due in months. When the bill lands, they just borrow again to cover it. The fast money was cheaper. So that’s what Washington took… in huge amounts. It works like a mortgage with a teaser rate. Your payment is small for 2 years. Then it resets to whatever the market says. Millions of Americans took that deal before the 2008 crash, and many of them lost their homes. Washington took the same deal… for the whole country. Nobody stopped it. Politicians don’t win elections by slashing budgets. Instead, the country gambled on interest rates staying low… forever.

segments.titre: 9.1% inflation and the Fed's fastest rate hikes in 40 years
segments.resume: Rates did not stay low: the economy caught fire and prices rose 9.1% a year by June 2022. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates by more than 5 points over 16 months, the fastest rise in 40 years, which slowed price hikes but hurt the country.
segments.texte: They didn’t. The economy caught fire. Prices skyrocketed. Millions of ordinary Americans saw their household bills surge out of control. By June 2022, prices were rising at 9.1% a year. To stop the whole thing from burning to the ground, the Federal Reserve did the only thing it could. It raised interest rates. Over the course of 16 months, the rates increased by more than 5 full points. It was the fastest rise in 40 years. Price hikes began to slow,

segments.titre: Interest cost jumps from $375 billion to $963 billion
segments.resume: The cheap short-term pandemic debt falls due with no cash to cover it, so the Treasury must sell new bonds, but the 1.5% rate is gone and investors now want 4%. Servicing the debt cost $375 billion in 2019 and reached $963 billion by July 2026, close to $1 trillion.
segments.texte: but the move hurt the country. All that cheap, short term pandemic debt is due and there’s no cash to cover it. That means the Treasury has to print and sell new bonds to make the payment. Except it’s not that easy. That 1.5% rate doesn’t exist anymore. Today’s investors want more. 4% to be exact. And they get it. And that adds more to the bill. In 2019, servicing the national debt cost the government $375 billion. By July 2026, it was $963 billion. The interest payments are close to $1 trillion.

segments.titre: Interest is now the second biggest government expense
segments.resume: Interest is the second biggest item of federal spending, behind only Social Security, and exceeds the Department of Defense and Homeland Security combined. It takes nearly 20 cents of every tax dollar collected, about $3,000 per American per year.
segments.texte: Interest is now the second biggest thing the government spends money on. Only Social Security beats it. It’s more than the cost of the Department of Defense and Homeland Security… combined. Right now, the interest bill steals nearly 20 cents of every single dollar the government collects from taxpayers. Split that across the entire population and every American covers roughly $3,000 a year.

segments.titre: Treasury auctions and the risk of buyers not showing up
segments.resume: Economists say America can carry debt forever thanks to its reserve currency status, but the plan eventually catches up. The Treasury pays off old bonds by auctioning new ones (444 auctions in 2025, about 9 a week); if buyers do not show up it must hike the rate, which is added to the debt for years with no announcement.
segments.texte: Economists will say a country like America can carry debt forever because it prints the world’s reserve economy. And for decades, they were right. But eventually, that plan catches up with you. When it comes to clearing debt, the government doesn’t pay off old bonds with cash. It auctions off fresh ones to somebody else. In 2025, the Treasury held 444 auctions, about 9 every week. Each one puts a set amount of new debt up for sale. If plenty of buyers turn up, the government borrows cheaply. But if the buyers don’t show up, the government has to lure them in somehow. To convince someone to buy that debt, the government is forced to hike the interest rate. That rate gets added to the national debt for years. There’s no announcement. No front page headlines. You’re just expected to deal with the fallout.

segments.titre: $9.6 trillion of debt maturing in 2026
segments.resume: The debt maturing in 2026 stands at $9.6 trillion and the Treasury must find a buyer for every dollar. If it fails, the government runs out of cash for pensions, military payrolls and medical coverage.
segments.texte: The total amount of debt maturing in 2026 stands at $9.6 trillion. And the Treasury has to find a buyer for every single dollar. If it doesn’t, the government runs out of cash to cover things like pensions, military payrolls and medical coverage.

segments.titre: A quarter of the debt exposed to the market: the Treasury is trapped
segments.resume: Short-term borrowing, the Treasury's financial shock absorber, rose from around 15% to about 25% of the debt, the highest since the 2008 crash. The Treasury cannot lock it all into 30-year fixed bonds without crashing the market and exploding rates, so it is trapped at the mercy of the market.
segments.texte: Treasury officials call this kind of short term borrowing their financial shock absorber. It used to make up a fraction of the nation’s debt, around 15%. Today, it’s closer to 25%, the highest since the 2008 crash. That means a quarter of America’s debt is exposed to brutal market forces. They can’t just lock it into 30 year fixed bonds. Dumping that amount of debt all at once, would cause the market to crash. Interest rates would explode. So they’re trapped. Loans that were agreed when money was practically free, now they are at the mercy of the market.

segments.titre: Mortgage rates: $1,300 more every month
segments.resume: When Washington pays more, everybody pays more. Between 2021 and 2023 mortgage rates jumped from about 2.65% to nearly 7.8%, roughly $1,300 more every month on a $400,000 loan, all because the government's borrowing costs moved.
segments.texte: And when Washington has to pay more, so does everybody else. Including you. Between 2021 and 2023, mortgage rates jumped from about 2.65% to nearly 7.8%. On a $400,000 loan, that’s roughly $1,300 more every month. All because the government’s borrowing costs moved.

segments.titre: $40 trillion of debt: borrowing to pay the interest on old debt
segments.resume: The government is like someone taking a cash advance on a new credit card to pay the minimum on an old one: the debt does not shrink while rates rise. The national debt crossed $40 trillion in August 2026, America borrowed more in 10 years than in its first 2 centuries, and cancelling every program would change nothing because interest contracts are legally binding.
segments.texte: It’s almost like taking a cash advance on a new credit card to pay the minimum payment on an old one. Your total debt doesn’t shrink, but the interest rates go up. That’s what the U.S. government is doing. It’s borrowing hundreds of billions to cover the interest on the old debt. In August 2026, the national debt crossed $40 trillion. America has borrowed as much in the last 10 years than it did in its first 2 centuries combined. Even if the government cancelled every single program, scaled back the military and sent the entire federal workforce home tomorrow, it would change a thing. The interest contacts are legally binding. The cash has to come from somewhere. And that demand is creating friction.

segments.titre: Treasury versus Fed: no third option
segments.resume: The Treasury needs cheap money to refinance and cannot skip a payment, while the Fed refuses to cut rates to keep inflation under control. If rates stay high, interest payments spiral out of control; if the Fed cuts aggressively and prints dollars to buy unwanted bonds, the purchasing power of your money is obliterated. There is no third option.
segments.texte: On one side you’ve got the Treasury. It desperately needs cheap money to refinance the debt. Skipping a payment would be catastrophic for the American economy. On the other side is the Federal Reserve. Its job is to keep your grocery bill under control. To stop inflation, the Fed is refusing to cut rates. It’s a necessary sacrifice that it feels it has to make. Neither side can give the other what it wants without committing self-sabotage. If interest rates remain high, the refinancing of debt continues at crippling prices. The interest payments add up, until the spiral out of control and everything comes crashing to the ground. The second option sees the Fed aggressively cutting rates and printing more dollars to buy up the bonds no one wants. But it also obliterates the purchasing power of the money in your wallet. There’s no third option. That’s the dilemma America is facing.

segments.titre: Forecast: $2.1 trillion of interest a year by 2036
segments.resume: Government analysts expect the annual interest bill to reach $2.1 trillion by 2036, roughly double today's level. If rates end up one point higher than forecast, another $3.2 trillion is added to the bill over the decade.
segments.texte: Government analysts expect the annual interest bill to reach $2.1 trillion a year by 2036. That’s roughly double where it stands now. And if interest rates rise one point higher than forecast, another $3.2 trillion is added to the bill over the decade.

segments.titre: Foreign buyers back away: Japan, Britain, China
segments.resume: The government relies on buyers snapping up its debt, but they are backing away. Japan, the biggest foreign holder with $1.14 trillion, is selling US bonds to protect the yen; Britain is second and China has trimmed holdings for years. Each sale pushes prices down and forces higher rates, and the debt ends up absorbed by American banks, funds and savers.
segments.texte: Essentially, the government is relying on buyers snapping up the debt. But they’re backing away. Right now Japan is the biggest foreign holder, sitting on $1.14 trillion of American government debt. The yen has been under strain, and to protect its collapsing currency, Tokyo is selling off American bonds for cash. Britain sits second on that list and has been dealing with the effects of a post Brexit world, while China has spent years trimming its holdings. Every time a foreign power dumps American bonds, the price gets pushed down further. And every time, Washington is forced to hike the interest rates. And the bill that lands on the Treasury’s desk gets bigger. When foreign buyers step back, that debt doesn’t disappear. It gets soaked up closer to home, by American banks, funds, and savers. This ties even more of your money to the government’s ability to keep paying.

segments.titre: July 2026 deficit and Ray Dalio's heart attack warning
segments.resume: The government spent $432 billion more than it collected in July 2026, the fourth worst month in its history, and ran $1.8 trillion short over the first 10 months of the budget year. Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio says this ends with a heart attack brought on by debt.
segments.texte: Meanwhile, the gap keeps widening while everyone argues over how to solve the problem. The government spent $432 billion more than it collected in July 2026. That was the fourth worst month in the country’s history. It came up $1.8 trillion short over the first 10 months of the budget year. Investor and founder of the hedge fund Bridgewater, Ray Dalio made a successful career from analysing the market. He spent 40 years betting on which countries pay their bill and now he’s looking at America’s tab. He says this ends with a heart attack brought on by debt.

segments.titre: 1942: the Fed caps interest rates to pay for the war
segments.resume: In April 1942, four months into the war, the Treasury needed to borrow more than anyone in history. The Fed agreed to hold short borrowing at three-eighths of 1% and cap long bonds at 2.5%, printing money to buy bonds whenever sellers pushed rates up. The war got paid for, and ordinary families put up the money.
segments.texte: But America has been here before. In April 1942, the U.S. was 4 months into a war it had to pay for. The Treasury needed to borrow more money than anyone ever had in human history. There wasn’t a market on earth that was large enough to lend as cheaply as America wanted. Left alone, interest rates would have climbed until the war itself was out of reach. So the Fed agreed to hold short government borrowing at three-eighths of 1%. It also capped the rate on long bonds at 2.5%. On paper it was just a technical arrangement between 2 agencies. Whatever the market wanted, that was the price people got. When sellers pushed rates up, the Fed just printed money to buy bonds until they fell again. It worked exactly as designed. The war got paid for, and it was ordinary families who put up the money.

segments.titre: Caps kept after the war: 17.6% inflation eats the war bonds
segments.resume: The rate caps stayed on for 6 more years after the war because nobody wanted to give the Treasury a higher bill. Prices rose 17.6% in a single year while war bonds were locked at wartime rates; the government never defaulted but repaid in dollars that bought a fraction of what they used to.
segments.texte: When the war ended, the government didn’t realise the shackles. The interest rate caps stayed on for 6 more years. Nobody in power wanted to hand the Treasury a higher bill. So the ceiling never came off. And that decision crushed the families who had bought into the war effort and snapped up the bonds. Prices skyrocketed by 17.6% in a single year. Those war bonds were still locked at their wartime rate, and the money inside them shrank. Technically no one defaulted. The government paid back every single bond in full, right on schedule. But they paid it back in dollars that bought a fraction of what they used to.

segments.titre: The grandfather's 1943 war bond
segments.resume: A grandfather buys a bond in 1943 to help pay for the Normandy landings, holds it 10 years and receives every cent promised. By then the money cannot buy a house, a car or the future he planned, and nobody who bought a bond was told.
segments.texte: Say your grandfather bought a bond in 1943, sold to him at a school hall or a factory gate. He wanted to do his bit and help pay for the landings in Normandy. He held it for 10 years. He trusted the system. And he received every cent he was promised. But by the time he got his money back, those cents couldn’t buy a house, a car or the future he’d spent a decade planning for. Nobody who bought a bond was told.

segments.titre: 1951: Truman versus the Fed and bankruptcy without the word default
segments.resume: In January 1951, with prices climbing again, President Truman told the Fed committee to keep the caps, and the Fed refused and fought back. It only won back the right to set rates in March 1951, after savers had been wiped out. The author calls this the playbook politicians use today: the only form of bankruptcy where nobody has to say the word default.
segments.texte: Behind the scenes, the Fed spent years trying to break the agreement. By January 1951, prices were climbing again, so President Truman called the whole committee to the White House and told them to keep the caps in place. He wanted cheap debt and didn’t care about the consequences. The Fed refused. They fought back. It took until March 1951 for the Fed to win back the right to set rates on its own. But by the time it won that bureaucratic battle, American savers had already been wiped out. It’s the same playbook politicians use today. Because it’s the only form of bankruptcy where nobody has to stand behind a podium and utter the word default.

segments.titre: Critics' argument: post-war debt, but America had the baby boom
segments.resume: Critics argue that America came out of World War II owing more than a year of output and climbed out without a collapse. The author replies that it was saved by the baby boom, a post-war manufacturing boost and a younger workforce, while today the workforce is aging, birth rates are declining and spending is on autopilot.
segments.texte: Critics will argue that history proves the debt not as bad as it seems. America came out of World War II owing way more than the country produced in a year. It held that massive amount of debt for decades and managed to climb out the financial hole without a catastrophic collapse. And it’s true. But they ignore the fact that America had help. It was saved by the baby boom. The economy had a post-war manufacturing boost and a younger workforce. It was a golden era for the economy. Today, that is completely reversed. The workforce is aging rapidly, birth rates are declining, and the government's spending seems to be on autopilot. And you just have to accept it.

segments.titre: No public vote: the slow loss of purchasing power
segments.resume: There will be no public vote on the national debt; it will happen behind closed doors and people will only notice at the local store or the gas pump. Buying power is reduced, savings lose value daily, and when you shrink the dollar you shrink the promise.
segments.texte: There’s not going to be a public vote on the national debt. It’ll happen behind closed doors, in rooms you’ll never have access to. The only time you’ll realize it is at the local store or the gas pump. Buying power is reduced, money doesn’t go as far and savings lose their value on a daily basis. When you shrink the dollar, you shrink the promise. Your bank balance remains the same, but the world moves a little further out of reach.

segments.titre: Who rides it out: real assets versus raw dollars
segments.resume: People who own land, stocks or commercial property can ride it out, while millions of families holding raw dollars feel the effect. Investors are already seeing warning signs and moving money into gold and other resources that hold their value.
segments.texte: People who have land, stocks or commercial property will be able to ride it out. But the millions of families who hold raw dollars are the ones who feel the effect. Investors are already seeing the warning signs. They’re cashing out and moving their money into gold or other resources that hold their value.

segments.titre: $117,000 per person, $297,000 per household
segments.resume: The debt works out to about $117,000 for every person and roughly $297,000 for every household. Nobody signed up for it: it was borrowed in citizens' names, one auction at a time, on a schedule that never stops and never asks for permission.
segments.texte: The debt works out to about $117,000 for every person in this country. Roughly $297,000 for every household. Nobody signed up for it. It was borrowed in your name while you were at work, one auction at a time, on a schedule that never stops. It never asks for your permission.

segments.titre: Conclusion: the interest rate time bomb and the bill for everyone
segments.resume: Politicians only care that the system survives, and fresh money has to arrive before the old promises come due. The interest rate time bomb is already going off, citizens' hard earned dollars are the only thing left to pay it with, and the system can neither be fixed nor voted out: there is no version where you do not pay for America's debt.
segments.texte: Politicians don’t care about your tax bracket. They don’t care about the zeros in your bank account. All they care about is that the system survives. And to do that, fresh money has to arrive before the old promises come due. The interest rate time bomb is already going off. The timer has hit zero. Your hard earned dollars are the only thing left to pay it with. The economic machine is insatiable. It will keep feeding until there's nothing of real value left in your account. The system can’t be fixed. It can’t be voted out. And it won’t spare you. There's no version of this where you don't pay for America’s debt.
